title: Hand Up the Credit So Your Wins Get Rewarded
hook: You just landed the win of the year. Tell the story the obvious way, and your boss will quietly stop helping you.
counterintuition: Many people think great work speaks for itself and bosses will happily reward it. Actually, your win pays off when it makes your boss look good, because the people above you want to feel they still stand higher.
keyTakeaway: When you win something big, give part of the glory to your boss, so your success makes them shine.
tryThisNow: Before your next meeting today, write down one thing your boss did that made your latest win possible.

memorableLines.text: Tell your wins so the person above you looks smart for backing you.

breakdown.fastRead:
Maya has just landed the biggest client her team has ever had. On Monday she plans to walk the whole meeting through it, step by step. Her manager, at the head of the table, is already smiling a little too tightly. Maya expects a raise. At school, good work got a good grade.

Work is not school. Your reward is decided by a person, and that person has pride. Shine alone, and the boss looks small beside you. Galileo learned this about money. He gave his inventions to many patrons, and each sent a gift and nothing more. Then he found four moons circling Jupiter, the symbol of the Medici family, and he named the moons after them. Cosimo II de' Medici made him the family's official scientist, with a steady salary. The discovery paid because it made his patrons look grand.

So Maya still tells the story on Monday. She opens it with the push her manager gave her and the door her manager opened. The facts stay the same. Only the order changes, and now the manager has a reason to back her next time. Share your big wins so they shine on the person above you, and the reward comes back to you.

breakdown.fullRead:
Maya has just landed the biggest client her team has ever had. On Monday she plans to walk the whole meeting through it, step by step. Her manager, at the head of the table, is already smiling a little too tightly. Maya expects this story to earn her a raise. It is about to make her manager feel like the least useful person in the room. Nobody will say so out loud, and that silence is part of the trouble.

Her hope makes sense, because it is how school worked. You did good work, the teacher saw it, and you got the grade. Work is not school. Your reward is decided by a person with feelings, not by the quality of the work alone, and bosses have their own pride. Shine too brightly alone, and they look small standing next to you. A worker who keeps outshining the boss in meetings often finds the best projects quietly going elsewhere. Nobody says why. The worker blames bad luck.

The people above you want to feel they stand higher, and that holds even when they like you. Almost everyone carries some doubt about their own talent, and people in high places want to feel secure and superior. So a boss who is fond of you can still turn on you once you make them feel second best. You can even outshine a boss without trying, simply by being quick or charming in the room. Some bosses are more unsure of themselves than others, and you cannot assume yours is the calm kind. A favor from a boss is no free pass either. Never let it go to your head.

The sharpest warning is Nicolas Fouquet, who ran the money for King Louis XIV of France. Fouquet was rich and charming, but he was passed over for prime minister and sensed the king's favor slipping. He wanted to win it back. So he held the grandest party anyone had seen, at a splendid new home, with the king as guest of honor. There was a rich meal, new music, a new play, beautiful gardens and fireworks, and the best minds of Europe came to enjoy it. Fouquet expected thanks. The next morning the king's men arrested him.

He was tried for stealing from the country and locked away in a far-off prison for the rest of his life. The party had been meant as a gift, but every guest spent the night admiring the host. Louis was proud and wanted to be the center of every room, so the evening felt like an insult. The king then hired the same designers to build something even grander, the palace of Versailles. Fouquet thought showing taste and wealth would win the king over. It only made the king feel smaller.

Galileo had the same problem, and his was about money. He needed steady support for his research, but he gave his inventions to many different patrons. Each one sent a gift. None of them took him on for good. Then he found four moons circling Jupiter. Jupiter was the Medici family's symbol, so he named the moons after them and offered the find as a sign of their greatness. Cosimo II de' Medici made him the family's official scientist, with a steady salary. Many small gifts had brought him nothing steady. One honor aimed at one family changed his life, because it made his patrons look grand instead of making him look grander. Fouquet's brilliance pushed the king into the shade. Galileo's brilliance lit up the family above him.

None of this means doing worse work. It means being careful how much of your talent you display to those above you. Galileo's moons were real, and the find was still his own. Stars can be as bright as the sun, but you never see them beside it in the sky. So be as strong as you are, and find ways to make the person above you look stronger. If your idea is better, link it to something your boss already said. If you know more, ask for their advice now and then, so they get to feel like the teacher. The same goes at home, where a parent or an aunt who has long run things can feel pushed aside by your quick fix.

So Maya still tells the story of the client, in a different order. She opens with the push her manager gave her and the door her manager opened. The facts of the win stay the same. Now the manager looks smart for backing her, and has a reason to speak up for her next time. The team still learns who did the work, because she is the one telling it. Share your big wins so they shine on the person above you, and the reward comes back to you.

examples.title: A sales deal closed alone
examples.scenario: Priya spent three months chasing a big client, and this morning the client finally signed. The team meeting starts in five minutes, and Priya's manager will ask how the deal came together. She did most of the work, so it feels fair to tell it as a solo win. She stands up, ready to speak, and has to choose what to say first.
examples.whatToDo: Open by thanking the manager for giving you the account and the room to chase it, then walk through how the deal came together.
examples.whyItMatters: The manager now looks smart for trusting her, so they will want to back her on the next big client.

examples.title: The science fair, one year later
examples.scenario: Last spring Marcus won the school science fair and told the local paper the idea was all his own. His teacher had stayed late twice to help, and after the article she stopped offering him the lab. This year his water filter has won again. The same reporter is walking over with a notebook.
examples.whatToDo: Name the teacher in your first answer, and say the late sessions with her are where the idea took shape.
examples.whyItMatters: A teacher who looks good in print opens the lab again and writes the stronger reference letter.

examples.title: Who saved the reunion?
examples.scenario: Leah's aunt has hosted the family reunion for ten years, and this year the rented hall fell through. Leah found a park pavilion and sorted out the food in two days. Now a cousin has posted in the group chat, "Finally, someone competent is in charge." Leah feels a rush of pride. Her aunt, who always answers within a minute, has said nothing.
examples.whatToDo: Post that you only followed your aunt's playbook, and ask her to give the welcome toast like every year.
examples.whyItMatters: The aunt still feels like the host, so Leah gains an ally at the picnic instead of a hurt relative.

questions.prompt: You led a new city park project, and it opens to big crowds. The mayor's office asks your department head for a statement. What do you do?
choices: Draft a statement your department head can give, built around the plan they approved.
Offer to give the statement yourself, since you know the project's details best.
Send your department head a full report of everything you did, so they have the facts.
questions.explanation: Drafting it for your department head makes the park their win too. Offering to speak yourself sounds helpful, but it puts you in the light and leaves them standing beside you.

questions.prompt: A baker's assistant invents a pastry that sells out daily and puts their own name on the menu card. The owner cuts their hours. What belief led them wrong?
choices: Believing the owner was too busy in the shop to notice a small change to the menu card.
Believing the pastry needed a name on the card to help it sell even better.
Believing a hit pastry would please the owner with only the assistant's name on it.
questions.explanation: The pastry was fine. The trap was expecting the owner to enjoy a success that carried someone else's name in their own shop. Whether the owner noticed the card was never the question.

questions.prompt: A front desk worker gets glowing guest reviews. At the next staff meeting they say the reviews show the manager's training works. What most likely happens next?
choices: The manager feels flattered for a day, and nothing about the worker's shifts changes.
The manager starts giving the worker better shifts, since the reviews now reflect on both.
The other staff come to resent the flattery, and the manager keeps the worker at a distance.
questions.explanation: Tying the reviews to the training gives the manager a share in them, so backing the worker now pays off for both. It would only read as flattery if the win behind it were not real.

questions.prompt: A reporter friend says, "My scoop is all over the internet, so my editor will be thrilled and hand me the next big story." What is your best reply?
choices: "Ask for the next big story right now, while the scoop is still fresh."
"Tell people how your editor's push shaped it, so the scoop is theirs too."
"Keep quiet about the scoop for a while, so your editor doesn't feel shown up."
questions.explanation: Crediting the editor's push lets the scoop make them look good. Staying quiet goes too far, because a win has to be seen to help anyone. Asking for more right away only puts the editor on the spot.

questions.prompt: A designer names their winning app feature after their manager's favorite project. Soon the manager gives them a lead role. Why did this work?
choices: The win now made the manager look good, so backing the designer helped the manager too.
The manager finally saw how skilled the designer was, and skill like that gets promoted.
The manager enjoyed the flattery, so the quality of the feature mattered very little.
questions.explanation: The feature was just as good before it had that name. What changed is that the manager gained from its success. Flattery alone would not have done it, because the win had to be real.

questions.prompt: Your idea for a new staff schedule saved your clinic money. Next week the clinic director reports the results to the board. What is your move before that meeting?
choices: Ask the director for five minutes at the board meeting to explain the schedule yourself.
Email the board a short note about the savings, and copy the director on it.
Give the director a one-page summary that ties the savings to their own goals.
questions.explanation: A summary built around the director's goals lets the savings make them shine. Copying them on a note to the board still goes around them, and they will feel it.

questions.prompt: A junior lawyer wins a case and thanks her mentor over coffee. In the firm newsletter she calls the win her own. The mentor grows distant. What is the trap?
choices: Thinking private thanks is enough when the public story leaves her mentor out.
Thinking the mentor's help was too small to deserve a place in the public story.
Thinking the firm newsletter was the wrong place to write about her win.
questions.explanation: The glory that counts is the kind other people see. Thanks over coffee did nothing for how the mentor looked to the firm. Leaving the win out of the newsletter would have helped nobody.

reviewCards.front: You're asked to give a short talk at the company party about the new app your team launched under your manager.
reviewCards.back: Open by thanking your manager's vision, then share your part, because a manager who shares the applause will want you on the next big project.

reviewCards.front: Your shop's sales doubled after your window display idea. Why would thanking the store manager in the staff meeting help your career?
reviewCards.back: Because the manager then looks like a smart leader for backing you, so they have a reason to reward you instead of feeling outdone.

reviewCards.front: When a grant you wrote gets approved and you announce it, the person to thank first is ...
reviewCards.back: ... the head of your group, because the win then adds to their name, and they become the one pushing for your next step.

reviewCards.front: A temp worker fixed a messy filing system in a week and expected a job offer, but the office head hired someone else.
reviewCards.back: They assumed good work gets rewarded by itself, but showing the office head how the fix made their office look better would have given them a reason to hire.

reviewCards.front: In your own words, what does 'hand up the credit' mean, and why does it work?
reviewCards.back: When you win big, share the glory with your boss so your success makes them shine, because a boss who looks good rewards you.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Tie your wins to your boss's goals, so your good work makes them look good in front of others.

ifThenPlans.context: When I write my weekly update for my boss
ifThenPlans.plan: then I open with what they set up or approved, and only then give my part.

ifThenPlans.context: When I notice I have told a win as if I did it alone
ifThenPlans.plan: then I tell the same people what my boss did to make it possible.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before you leave work today, open your last project update. Add one sentence that links the result to a goal your boss cares about, so they can pass it up the line.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each time you walk into your weekly check-in with your boss, bring one recent win. Show them how it helps their goals, so they can use it when they report to their own boss.
